title: Yahweh Watch Between Me and You — Flight, Pursuit, a Heap of Stones
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Our last lesson came to rest on three words: God remembered Rachel. In the chapter in front of us today, Jacob is about to leave Haran. Twenty years, four women, eleven children, and a very large flock of sheep. When he arrived, all he had was a staff.
And the question this lesson puts to you may sting a little: is there something you have said out loud that you handed over to God, and which is still sitting in your luggage?
Because in this chapter a whole family is travelling towards the land God promised them — and there are other gods hidden in the baggage.

Let me put the answer at the very front: when the circumstances change and the word of God arrives on top of it, the time has come. And yet on the road towards God, a person's hand is very often still closed around a spare insurance policy.
1. Two Signals Pointing the Same Way

Verses 1 and 2: "Jacob heard Laban's sons' words, saying, 'Jacob has taken away all that was our father's. He has obtained all this wealth from that which was our father's.' … Jacob saw the expression on Laban's face, and, behold, it was not toward him as before."

Brothers and sisters, the phrase behind "the expression on Laban's face" is in Hebrew פְּנֵי לָבָן — "the face of Laban." Hebrew constantly uses the face to speak of attitude and of relationship. That face had changed.
That is the first signal: the circumstances had changed.
Then verse 3: "Yahweh said to Jacob, 'Return to the land of your fathers, and to your relatives, and I will be with you.'"
That is the second signal: God had spoken.
Brothers and sisters, here is a very practical principle for discerning timing: a change in the circumstances plus a word from God — two signals pointing in the same direction.

But notice how much the pairing matters. If only the circumstances have changed, that may be nothing more than trouble with people, and not God telling you to go. If all you have is a vague inner stirring while the circumstances have not shifted an inch, then wait a little longer as well. And when the two of them line up with each other, that is usually the moment the time has come.
And in verse 13 the way God introduces himself is deeply moving: "I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar, where you vowed a vow to me."
Brothers and sisters, twenty years had gone by. That night of the vow. That stone he had put under his head. That sentence — "If God will be with me … Yahweh will be my God."
Jacob had very likely forgotten it long ago. And God says: I am the God of Bethel.

God remembers the vows we have made, even when we ourselves have forgotten them. And the way he remembers is not a rebuke — it is an introduction. He reminds Jacob by taking the name of that place for his own.
"The expression on Laban's face is not toward me as before" — plus God saying "Return." How do I tell a signal from my circumstances apart from the guidance of God?

This chapter gives us a very good pattern: two signals pointing in the same direction at the same time. Verse 2 is the circumstances — the face has changed, the wages have been changed ten times. Verse 3 is God speaking: "Return to the land of your fathers." And in verse 11 Jacob also mentions guidance that came to him in a dream. Add the three together and they all face the same way. The practical principle is this: never lean on only one of them. Circumstances going badly may be no more than difficulty, and not a summons to leave; a stirring in the heart may be no more than your own exhaustion. The safer method is to look for agreement between three things — the word of God, an open door in the circumstances, and the confirmation of mature people. When all three point the same way, you may move.
He talked the whole thing over with his two wives before he went. Does that detail matter?

It matters a great deal. Verse 4 says he sent and called Rachel and Leah out to the field where his flock was, and he laid the whole thing out for them: how Laban had treated him, how God had protected him, and what God had said. And they answered, "Now then, whatever God has said to you, do." A decision of that size, and he did not act first and inform them afterwards. This is well worth learning for any husband and any leader: tell the process to the people who will have to carry the consequences with you, and give them the chance to agree. A great many cracks in a family do not come from the decision being wrong; they come from somebody being told after the fact. Being of one mind is not requiring the other person to accept the outcome. It is letting him take part in the process.
Verses 36 to 42 are the first time in twenty years that Jacob says out loud what he has been holding in.
And this passage is worth reading slowly, because it is one of the most concrete descriptions of faithfulness in the whole Bible.

Verses 38 and 39: "These twenty years I have been with you. Your ewes and your female goats have not cast their young, and I haven't eaten the rams of your flocks. That which was torn of animals, I didn't bring to you. I bore its loss. Of my hand you required it, whether stolen by day or stolen by night."

Brothers and sisters, under the Near Eastern law of that period, when an animal had been torn by wild beasts the shepherd only had to bring back the carcass and he was cleared of liability. And Jacob says: I never did that. I bore the loss myself.
Verse 40: "This was my situation: in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep fled from my eyes."
Verse 41: "These twenty years I have been in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years for your flock, and you have changed my wages ten times."
Ten times he changed the wages.
Brothers and sisters, those were twenty deeply unfair years. And through all twenty of them Jacob did not steal, did not run, and did not take revenge — he simply went on shepherding the flock.

And in verse 42 he says the sentence that matters most: "Unless the God of my father … and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely now you would have sent me away empty. God has seen my affliction and the labor of my hands, and rebuked you last night."
"The fear of Isaac" — פַּחַד יִצְחָק, literally "the Fear of Isaac", the One whom Isaac feared. In the whole Bible that title appears only twice, and both times in this chapter.

Brothers and sisters, weigh this carefully: twenty years on, when the moment came to swear an oath, what he still said was "my father's God." On that night at Bethel he had said, "Yahweh will be my God" — but here, on his own lips, that God is still his father's God.
It will take the ford of the Jabbok, in the next chapter, before he truly meets him for himself.
Jacob lays out twenty years of accounts. Does that count as complaining?

From verse 36 he goes on for ten verses without drawing breath, pouring out twenty years of grievance: the drought consuming him by day, the frost by night, sleep fleeing from his eyes, his wages changed ten times over. That is complaining, and it is also the plain truth. And Scripture writes it down just as it stands. What is worth noticing is who he complains to: he says it to Laban's face, not behind his back to somebody else. That gives us a very practical principle. What needs saying should be said face to face, because only after it has been said is reconciliation possible at all; say it behind a man's back for twenty years and the account only compounds. Of course the manner of saying it should leave the other person some room — and this chapter does in fact end in a covenant.
3. A Light from the Original: the God Hidden Under a Camel's Saddle
Now we come to the shortest verse in this chapter, and the heaviest.
Verse 19: "Now Laban had gone to shear his sheep; and Rachel stole the teraphim that were her father's."

Brothers and sisters, the word for those images is תְּרָפִים (*teraphim*) — the household guardian gods; archaeological finds show that they were usually small enough to be picked up and held in the hand.

And scholars point out that in the Near Eastern documents of that period, possession of the household gods may have been bound up with the right of inheritance to the family estate. So some say she took them for the property. Others say she took them to get back at her father.
But I want to point out a clue that matters more. In Genesis 35:2 Jacob says to his whole household, "Put away the foreign gods that are among you."
And that is already several years later.
Which is to say: those images travelled with them for a very long time.
Brothers and sisters, this family is walking towards the land God promised them, and there are other gods hidden in the luggage.

And the scene in verses 34 and 35 is written with a very sharp edge. Laban goes into the tent and searches: "Now Rachel had taken the teraphim, put them in the camel's saddle, and sat on them. Laban felt around all the tent, but didn't find them." And she says to her father, "Don't let my lord be angry that I can't rise up before you; for I'm having my period."
A god that has to be sat on before it can stay hidden.

Isaiah 46:1–2 says it more savagely still: "Bel bows down. Nebo stoops. Their idols are carried by animals, and on the livestock. The things that you carried around are heavy loads, a burden for the weary. They stoop and they bow down together. They could not deliver the burden, but they have gone into captivity."
Brothers and sisters, that is what an idol is at bottom: you think it is protecting you, and in fact you are the one carrying it.

And let me bring this closer to home. The household gods of today do not look like that. It may be a sum of money in an account you dare not touch — because of "just in case." It may be a relationship you have kept on hold — because of "in case." It may be a fallback plan, an escape route, one thing you have never actually handed over.
An idol is not defined as "a bad thing." An idol is that one insurance policy you keep in case God should turn out not to work.
Rachel stole her father's household gods. Why is that written up in such detail?

Those household gods (תְּרָפִים) may in that society have functioned as the title deeds to the family inheritance, so this was not only a religious matter but a property matter. And the tension in the text lies here: Jacob does not know. He says, "Anyone you find your gods with shall not live" — which means that without meaning to he has just cursed the person he loves most. More unsettling still, this family is walking towards the promised land with idols in the luggage, and it is not until chapter 35 that those things are finally buried under the oak at Shechem. What that says to us is this: a person can be walking in the right direction and still be hiding something he has never dealt with.
Laban calls the images "my gods." What kind of faith is that?

In verse 30 he says, "why have you stolen my gods?" — a god that can be stolen. And Jacob names the One he trusts as "the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac." The contrast is deliberate: on the one side a god a man holds in his hand, on the other side the God who holds the man. This is very useful to us today, because we too can turn faith into something that is "mine": my peace, my blessing, my devotional routine. The way to test it is to ask: if this one thing were taken away from me, would I still worship? Whatever can be stolen from you is usually not God at all. It is an insurance policy we have made out of God.
4. Mizpah: Not a Blessing, a Ceasefire
In verse 44 Laban says, "Now come, let's make a covenant, you and I. Let it be for a witness between me and you."
They gathered stones into a heap, and they ate a meal there. And then comes the sentence in verse 49 that a great many people have heard:
"and Mizpah, for he said, 'Yahweh watch between me and you, when we are absent one from another.'"
Brothers and sisters, that line has been printed on countless cards, hung on countless wall plaques, engraved on countless farewell keepsakes, and it is called "the Mizpah blessing."

But please read the next verse through to the end. Verse 50: "If you afflict my daughters, or if you take wives in addition to my daughters, no man is with us; behold, God is witness between me and you."
And verse 52: "May this heap be a witness, and the pillar be a witness, that I will not pass over this heap to you, and that you will not pass over this heap and this pillar to me, for harm."
Brothers and sisters, that is not a blessing. That is two men keeping watch on each other.
Two men, neither of them willing to come off worse and neither of them trusting the other, end up with nothing left to do but ask God to serve as the surveillance camera.
And let me say something very honest: as endings go, this one is actually not bad at all.

Because they did not come to blows. They stated the boundary plainly, they made a covenant, they ate a meal, and the next morning Laban "kissed his sons and his daughters, and blessed them. Laban departed and returned to his place."

Some relationships, here on earth, can only get this far. Not every rupture can be restored to closeness. Romans 12:18 puts it with real balance: "If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men." — and those four words, "if it is possible", are Scripture's own qualification, not ours.
The Mizpah line is usually treated as a blessing. It isn't one, is it?

Verse 49: "Yahweh watch between me and you, when we are absent one from another." And the next verse goes straight on to name what that watching is for: "If you afflict my daughters, or if you take wives in addition to my daughters, no man is with us; behold, God is witness between me and you." The setting is two men who do not trust each other making a covenant and going their separate ways. That is a ceasefire agreement, not a blessing. Today a great many people print it on a card for a friend who is going far away, and that is a misuse. But there is a very healthy lesson buried in it: not every relationship can be repaired all the way back to intimacy, and for some relationships the best available outcome is that neither party crosses the line. Admitting that is not failure. It is honesty. And notice that they piled up that heap of stones together and ate together — even a parting can be done in good order.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is treating the Mizpah line as a benediction for people who are parting. The context is two men who do not trust each other asking God to keep watch on each other, and verse 50 says so in perfectly plain words. Print it on a card as a blessing and you have read it exactly backwards. This is not to say the sentence may never be used — only that its original setting has to be stated honestly.

The second is preaching "God stopped Laban" as a guarantee that God will always take my side. In verse 24 God warns Laban in a dream, "Be careful that you don't speak to Jacob either good or bad." That was to protect his covenant and his plan; it was not God picking sides in every quarrel. Preach it as a guarantee and the congregation will start treating God as the muscle they bring along to a fight with other people.

The third is preaching leaving without a word as shrewdness. Verse 20 says he "deceived Laban the Syrian", and the Hebrew is literally "stole the heart of Laban" — the tone of it is negative. He was afraid, and that is understandable; but being afraid is not the same as being right. Dress it up as wisdom and you will raise a congregation that spends a lifetime dodging every conflict.

The fourth is treating Rachel's theft of the household gods as a trifle. In chapter 35 God tells them to put away the foreign gods, which shows that this matter dragged on for years. Pass over it lightly and nobody in the room will go and look inside his own luggage.

The fifth is preaching this chapter as the story of a good man who finally gets away from a bad boss. Laban really was unfair — but Jacob was not innocent either; in chapter 30 he worked the business with the rods so that only the strong animals came out his way. The point of this chapter is not who was right and who was wrong. It is how God kept a man safe inside an unfair relationship, and how, twenty years later, he called him back.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: I am in a workplace, or a family relationship, that is deeply unfair. However much I do, it is never acknowledged, and my wages have been changed ten times over. How long am I supposed to endure it? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives three very practical tests. First, while you are enduring, do your duty right to the end. In twenty years Jacob did not slack, did not take revenge and did not slip away — he even bore the loss himself for animals torn by wild beasts. So "I am going to leave" is never a licence to start coasting. Second, the timing of leaving needs two signals. The circumstances have changed (the expression on Laban's face), and the word of God has come (verse 3). If you have only one of the two, wait a little longer. Third, and most important of all: the way you leave matters enormously. Jacob ran off in secret, was pursued for seven days, and in the end still had to say everything out loud. Far better to say it properly at the start than to be overtaken and have to say it then. And let me add one thing: if what that relationship involves is harm and not merely unfairness — if you are being exploited, intimidated or oppressed — then you do not have to wait for two signals. Safety always comes first.

The second question: Chinese homes often keep a few things around "just in case" — a statue nobody has thrown out, a charm nobody has taken down, a membership nobody has cancelled, a fortune teller somebody habitually goes back to consult. Are these things really as serious as all that? Brothers and sisters, this chapter's answer is: the serious thing is not the object. The serious thing is the "just in case." Rachel carried those images for years and nothing went wrong the whole way — until chapter 35, when God said, "Put them away." And I want to point out two things. First, that phrase "just in case" is itself the problem. What it means is: I believe in God, but I do not believe in him entirely. Second, the way you deal with it must be gentle and clear at the same time. Jacob's method in chapter 35 was to deal with it as a whole household, and then go up to Bethel. He did not quietly throw the things away by himself, and he did not shame his family into handing them over. If the elders in your home are not yet believers, those objects are theirs, and you cannot throw them out on their behalf; but the part that belongs to you — that part you can deal with today.
The relationship with an elder, or with a boss, has broken down completely. How do I "end it well"?

Four practical steps. First, say the thing clearly, and say it face to face — state the facts, do not go after the person. Second, settle the accounts: give what should be given, return what should be returned, and leave no muddled ledger behind. Third, set a boundary and say it out loud — like that heap of stones, so that both sides know how things will run from here on. Fourth, bless where you can, and where you cannot, at the very least do not curse. And one thing must be added: if the other party is involved in violence, threats or anything unlawful, safety comes first — report what should be reported, seek the help that should be sought, and do not handle it alone. Ending well is not for the other person's sake. It is so that you can still walk afterwards.
7. Living 321 Out — Go Back and Make Good on That Vow
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — for twenty years the drought consumed Jacob by day and the frost by night, his wages were changed ten times, and he went on faithfully shepherding the flock. And Isaiah 53:3 says of the Lord Jesus that he was "a man of suffering and acquainted with disease"; 1 Peter 2:23 says that "when he was cursed, he didn't curse back. When he suffered, he didn't threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously." Brothers and sisters, my role model is this: inside unfairness he stayed faithful to the very end.

The Bible is my standard — in verse 13 God says, "I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar, where you vowed a vow to me." A standard has one function that is very seldom mentioned: it preserves the words we ourselves have spoken. The vow you made at some revival meeting, the thing you said to God beside a hospital bed, the prayer you prayed when your child was born — God remembers every one of them.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — the guidance in this chapter is the confluence of two signals: the circumstances changed, and the word of God came. Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit's guidance rarely arrives down a single channel. If all you have is a feeling with no confirmation from your situation, or a situation with no confirmation from the word, then wait a little longer.

Let Jesus be King — "I am the God of Bethel." To let Jesus be King is to go back and make good on that vow. And notice this: God did not come chasing Jacob for it in the second year after he made it. He waited twenty years, and then, just as Jacob was getting ready to move, he mentioned it quietly, in a single sentence.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — in verse 42 Jacob says, "Unless the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely now you would have sent me away empty." He credits twenty years of household wealth to God, and not to his own clever rods.

Establish God's system — the heap of stones at Mizpah bought a ceasefire, not a reconciliation. Brothers and sisters, some relationships here on earth can only get that far. To establish God's system is to learn to hold on to who it is you believe in even inside an imperfect relationship — you can set a clear boundary with someone and go your separate ways, and carry no bitterness in your heart at the same time.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We speak a great deal about selflessness and about denying of self, and this chapter adds something important to that. At the end Jacob settles twenty years of accounts with complete clarity, item by item, out loud. And God does not rebuke him for it. So selflessness does not mean you may never say what you have suffered. Stating a thing plainly and taking revenge are two entirely different things. A person who never dares to say "this is not fair" is very often not being humble — he is being afraid; and the grievance that never gets said out loud turns, in the end, into bitterness.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, the Same Luggage
Brothers and sisters, one and the same journey home, falling into four different hearts, gets packed with four different sets of luggage.

The proud heart says: "How could Rachel have been so foolish?" This heart finishes the chapter busy hunting for household gods in everybody else's luggage. Brothers and sisters, notice that the text never records Jacob knowing about it — he even says in verse 32, "Anyone you find your gods with shall not live." He had no idea there were any inside his own household. And the luggage we can see most easily is always somebody else's.

The fearful heart says: "Then what on earth am I still carrying?" This heart finishes the chapter and starts turning out every drawer and every box, growing more frantic the more it searches. To that heart I want to say: you do not have to find all of it at once. In chapter 35 it was when Jacob was about to go up to Bethel that God said, "Put away the foreign gods." God points it out at the right time, and when he points it out he usually gives you the next step along with it.

The ashamed heart says: "I have served all these years and I am still treated like this." You may be just like Jacob — the drought consuming you by day, the frost by night — and the person concerned has never once thanked you. Brothers and sisters, look carefully at verse 42: "God has seen my affliction and the labor of my hands." Your twenty years — there is Someone who has been keeping the record, item by item.

The wounded heart says: "That person and I can never go back to what we were." You may have a relationship you have tried and tried to mend and it will not mend. Brothers and sisters, what this chapter gives you is not a model of reconciliation. It is a model of a boundary. They piled up a heap of stones and said: I will not cross over to harm you, and you are not to cross over to harm me. And then each went his own way. That is not failure. That is how grown people part. And notice the last verse of the chapter: Laban "kissed his sons and his daughters, and blessed them." Even a relationship like that one can have a blessing at the end of it.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, go through your luggage. Take ten quiet minutes and ask God one question: Lord, what "just in case" am I still carrying? Then write down the one thing that floats to the surface.

Second, go back and find a vow you once made. Think about what you have said to God at some point — in your hardest season, when a child was born, after an illness lifted. This week, make good on one of them.

Third, say one unfair thing out loud. Not as revenge — as a plain statement. Find the right moment and the right person, and say the thing you have borne in silence for a long time, once, in a way that accuses nobody.

Fourth, pile up a heap of stones for a relationship that cannot go back. Write down the clear boundary between you and that person: I will not cross over, and I ask you not to cross over to me either. And once you have written it, bless him once.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church, in three sentences: there is a man in the Bible whose father-in-law changed his wages ten times, and he worked twenty years, hot by day, cold by night, unable to keep his eyes shut; when he was going home, his wife secretly hid her family's household gods under the camel's saddle and sat on top of them; and this is the line that has stayed with me — a god that has to be sat on before it can stay hidden, who exactly is it going to protect?
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will deal with that one insurance policy I keep in case God should turn out not to work.
I declare that I will go back and make good on the vow I once made, because he is the God of Bethel.
I declare that inside an unfair relationship I will still do my duty right to the end.
I declare that some relationships can go no further than a boundary, and that I can leave with a blessing and without bitterness.
This week I am supposed to say the thing that needs saying, face to face. But I am afraid a row will start the moment I open my mouth. What do I do?

Three preparations that genuinely help. First, write it down beforehand: put what you want to say into three sentences, read them over once, and take out every word that attacks the person. Second, choose the time and the setting: not at the dinner table, not with other people present, not late at night. Third, speak about the relationship before you speak about the matter — a sentence like "I care about our relationship, and that is exactly why I want to be clear with you about something" will bring the other person's defences down. And finally, accept this: the only thing you can control is how you say it, not how it is received. Once it has been said, hand that part over to God. If you know for certain that the other person will become agitated, you can ask someone you trust to be present, or arrange to meet in a slot that has to end within half an hour — a time limit by itself makes what you say shorter and more accurate.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, let it be the woman sitting on the camel's saddle.

Laban comes into the tent and feels his way over it, inch by inch. And she is sitting on that saddle-basket, perfectly composed, saying: don't let my lord be angry that I can't rise up before you; I'm having my period.
And underneath her, pressed flat, are her gods.
Brothers and sisters, the picture is very nearly comic: she is having to protect the very thing that was supposed to protect her.
And I want to ask you: is there anything in your luggage that you have to hold down with your own body — something nobody may see, something you dare not take out and hold up to the light?

It need not be a carved image. It may be a bank account, a habit, a relationship, an escape route. What they all have in common is this: your mouth says you trust God, and your luggage carries the thing anyway — because, just in case.

And the gentlest thing in this whole chapter is verse 13. God does not begin by going through their luggage. He says only one sentence: "I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar, where you vowed a vow to me."
He begins by reminding them of a night they once had — that night of the stone pillow and the opened heaven.

He wants them to go back. And on the way back the luggage will be dealt with, item by item — in chapter 35 they hand over those images, and Jacob hides them under the oak at Shechem, and only then do they go up to Bethel.

The focus is not on who wronged me for twenty years, not on what is hidden in my luggage, and not on whether that relationship can be mended. The focus is on Jesus — he is the God of Bethel, the Lord who remembers the vows we made and who comes himself to call us back. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to open our own luggage and look inside it once, and to go back and make good on one vow we made. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the ordinary days. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.

1. ★★★ The word of God, an open door in the circumstances, the confirmation of mature people — move only when all three point the same way. How does that principle apply to the decision that is in your hands right now?
2. ★★ He laid the whole thing out for his wives before he left. Is being of one mind about requiring the other person to accept the outcome, or about letting him take part in the process?
3. ★ Laban says "my gods"; Jacob says "the God of my father." What is the difference between a god that can be stolen and the God who holds on to a man?
4. ★★ Mizpah is not a blessing; it is a ceasefire. Why is admitting that some relationships can only reach a ceasefire also a form of honesty?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I put up with it for twenty years; that shows how generous I am), fearful (if I say it out loud I will lose this job or this relationship), ashamed (there is something hidden in my luggage too), wounded (my wages have been changed ten times). Which are you most like? And what experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Return to the land of your fathers, and to your relatives, and I will be with you." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there a ledger in your heart that you have been keeping for a very long time? Have you ever said it face to face? What is holding you back?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "What is still hidden in my luggage is …"
9. ★★ This week, to whom will you say, face to face, the one thing that needs saying? Write those three sentences down now, here in the room.

Leader's reminder: questions nine and eleven will touch long-standing grievances at work and in the family. Do not let the group pass comment on any named person. If threats, violence or anything unlawful is involved, remind him that safety comes first, and help him find the proper official channels.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own family, is there a relationship that needs to be "ended well", or to have its boundary stated plainly? Say what you are going to do.
